title: Sen. Jane M. Timken votes yea on SB102, a tax-foreclosure and land-reutilization bill
text:
Sen. Jane M. Timken votes yea on SB102, a tax-foreclosure and land-reutilization bill
T. T. Young
Sen. Jane M. Timken (R-29th) voted yea on SB102, a tax-foreclosure and land-reutilization bill that passed the Ohio Senate 33-0 on Wednesday, June 10, 2026, during the 136th Ohio General Assembly, according to the Ohio Legislature.
The following summary and breakdown are based on the bill's official text and include interpretations to clarify the measure's provisions.
The bill overhauls Ohio’s tax foreclosure and land reutilization laws, renaming them the Gus Frangos Act. It refines county foreclosure procedures, expands the use of county boards of revision, and tightens notice, service and redemption rules, including an “alternative redemption period” and a new right for interested parties to demand public auction. It broadens protections and tools for county land reutilization corporations, clarifies lien priority and environmental liability limits, and adjusts distributions of sale proceeds. The bill also creates a temporary tax exemption and payment-in-lieu system for properties conveyed by land banks, and makes conforming changes across related tax, nuisance and environmental statutes.
SB102 was introduced by Sen. Thomas F. Patton.
Timken was appointed to the Ohio State Senate to represent the 29th District and is the Republican national committeewoman for Ohio.
She served as chairman of the Ohio Republican Party from 2017 to 2021, becoming the first woman elected to that post.
Timken graduated cum laude from Harvard College and earned her J.D., summa cum laude, from American University, Washington College of Law.
She began her legal career with the firm Black McCuskey and served as a magistrate and law clerk to Judge Sara Lioi.
In Ohio, the legislative process begins when a bill is introduced in either the House of Representatives or the Senate. A bill must receive three considerations in each chamber, and it may be referred to a committee for hearings, debate and possible amendments before advancing to a floor vote. If both chambers pass the same version, the bill is sent to the governor, who can sign it, veto it or allow it to become law without a signature. The Ohio General Assembly begins a new legislative session every two years on the first Monday in January of odd-numbered years, and there is no limit on the number of days it may convene.
